newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plans money laundering rules for non-banks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plans money laundering rules for non-banks.

text.p: With illicit money laundering moving from highly regulated banks to local check cashing outlets and foreign currency changers, U.S. Treasury Department said Thursday it would release new reporting rules for non-bank transactions.

"As we have become more successful in the United States in dealing with cash and more effective in relationships with banks, it is not surprisng that we find oursleves dealing with non-cash and non-banks," said Stanley Morris, director of the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network known as FinCEN.

The proposed rules for non-banks, to be released for comment in a few weeks, will impose reporting requirements on check cashers and related firms similiar to those imposed on banks, Morris said at a Congressional hearing here.

The money service business handles $200 billion a year, Morris noted. "We've seen in a number places, like New York, abuses, so we have established a new set of regulations which will be out shortly," he said.
The rules will require firms to register with the government but will exclude businesses like supermarkets and hotels that have limited cash dealings, Morris said.
"We've worked very hard on the definitions," he said.

Firms will have to report large or "suspicious" money transfers, particularly those done by issuers of money orders, travellers checks and money remittances, Morris said. Remittances of money out of the country will also be reported, he added.
Once the rules are released, there will be a comment period of about 90 days.
"We fully expect by the end of the year to have this industry clearly within the same confines as we have our nation's banks in," Morris said.
